person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: THE CONSENSUS CONFERENCE THAT WROTE RIFLE - a two-day meeting that turned more than thirty competing definitions of acute renal failure into one five-level classification, and published it as a hypothesis to be tested
span.quote: There is no consensus definition of acute renal failure (ARF) in critically ill patients. More than 30 different definitions have been used in the literature, creating much confusion and making comparisons difficult.

span.label: what a definition of acute renal failure must do, and whether one can be agreed at all when more than thirty are in use
span.quote: In addition, we considered that the following features would be important in any definition of ARF: it should consider change from baseline; it should include classifications for acute on chronic renal disease; it should be easy to use and clinically applicable across different centres; and it should consider both sensitivity and specificity because of different populations and research questions.

span.label: the RIFLE classification - Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, End-stage - plus consensus on outcome measures, physiological end-points, animal models and fluid therapy across 47 questions
span.quote: In addition to the three levels of renal dysfunction, the RIFLE (acronym indicating Risk of renal dysfunction; Injury to the kidney; Failure of kidney function, Loss of kidney function and End-stage kidney disease) criteria also include two clinical outcomes: 'loss' and 'end-stage renal disease' (ESRD). These are separated to acknowledge the important adaptations that occur in ESRD that are not seen in persistent ARF. Persistent ARF (loss) is defined as need for renal replacement therapy (RRT) for more than 4 weeks, whereas ESRD is defined by need for dialysis for longer than 3 months.

span.label: method
span.quote: In addition to the three levels of renal dysfunction, the RIFLE (acronym indicating Risk of renal dysfunction; Injury to the kidney; Failure of kidney function, Loss of kidney function and End-stage kidney disease) criteria also include two clinical outcomes: 'loss' and 'end-stage renal disease' (ESRD). These are separated to acknowledge the important adaptations that occur in ESRD that are not seen in persistent ARF. Persistent ARF (loss) is defined as need for renal replacement therapy (RRT) for more than 4 weeks, whereas ESRD is defined by need for dialysis for longer than 3 months.

span.label: a disease whose boundary had to be voted on before it could be studied
span.quote: The clinical condition of ARF is said to occur in anywhere from 1% to 25% of critically ill patients [ 1 , 2 ], depending on the population being studied and the criteria used to define its presence. Furthermore, mortality in these populations ranges from 28% to 90% [ 10 , 11 ]. Clearly, trials of prevention and therapy are not comparable because widely disparate definitions have been used.

span.label: consensus conference: six workgroups, literature searches, alternating breakout and plenary sessions, correspondence where consensus failed, and a two-thirds majority where a vote was needed
span.term: consensus conference: six workgroups, literature searches, alternating breakout and plenary sessions, correspondence where consensus failed, and a two-thirds majority where a vote was needed
span.quote: When consensus was not achieved on any individual question by the conclusion of the meeting, deliberations continued by correspondence. When voting was required to settle an issue, a two-thirds majority was required to approve a proposal.

span.label: THE CLAIM PAPER 50 OPENS WITH, AT ITS SOURCE: `There is NO CONSENSUS DEFINITION of acute renal failure in critically ill patients. MORE THAN 30 DIFFERENT DEFINITIONS have been used in the literature, CREATING MUCH CONFUSION AND MAKING COMPARISONS DIFFICULT.` The corpus now holds the claim and the paper that made it
span.quote: There is no consensus definition of acute renal failure (ARF) in critically ill patients. More than 30 different definitions have been used in the literature, creating much confusion and making comparisons difficult.

span.label: AND THE NUMBERS DIFFER FROM THE VALIDATION PAPER'S: here `ARF is said to occur in anywhere from 1% TO 25% of critically ill patients ... Furthermore, MORTALITY in these populations RANGES FROM 28% TO 90% ... TRIALS OF PREVENTION AND THERAPY ARE NOT COMPARABLE BECAUSE WIDELY DISPARATE DEFINITIONS HAVE BEEN USED`. hoste2006, two years later, gives 1-31% and 19-83% for the same claim. **THE RANGE OF THE RANGE VARIES** - both are ranges over different reference sets and both are presented as the state of the literature
span.quote: The clinical condition of ARF is said to occur in anywhere from 1% to 25% of critically ill patients [ 1 , 2 ], depending on the population being studied and the criteria used to define its presence. Furthermore, mortality in these populations ranges from 28% to 90% [ 10 , 11 ]. Clearly, trials of prevention and therapy are not comparable because widely disparate definitions have been used.

span.label: AND THE COMMITTEE PUBLISHES A SPECIFICATION FOR WHAT A DEFINITION MUST DO: `it should CONSIDER CHANGE FROM BASELINE; it should include classifications for ACUTE ON CHRONIC renal disease; it should be EASY TO USE AND CLINICALLY APPLICABLE ACROSS DIFFERENT CENTRES; and it should CONSIDER BOTH SENSITIVITY AND SPECIFICITY because of different populations and research questions`. Four requirements, written down before the classification
span.quote: In addition, we considered that the following features would be important in any definition of ARF: it should consider change from baseline; it should include classifications for acute on chronic renal disease; it should be easy to use and clinically applicable across different centres; and it should consider both sensitivity and specificity because of different populations and research questions.

span.label: and the multilevel design IS the sensitivity/specificity trade-off, made explicit: the scheme must `detect patients in whom renal function is MILDLY AFFECTED (HIGH SENSITIVITY ... BUT LIMITED SPECIFICITY) and patients in whom renal function is MARKEDLY AFFECTED (HIGH SPECIFICITY ... BUT LIMITED SENSITIVITY)`
span.quote: A classification system should therefore include and separate mild (or early) and severe (or late) cases. This will allow such a classification to detect patients in whom renal function is mildly affected (high sensitivity for the detection of kidney malfunction but limited specificity for its presence) and patients in whom renal function is markedly affected (high specificity for true renal dysfunction but limited sensitivity in picking up early and subtler loss of function). Accordingly, we advocate a multilevel classification system in which a wide range of disease spectra can be included.

span.label: AND THE MARKER THE DEFINITION IS BUILT ON IS ADMITTED TO BE WRONG IN EXACTLY THIS CONDITION: `the serum creatinine WILL NOT BE AN ACCURATE REFLECTION OF GFR IN THE NON-STEADY-STATE CONDITION OF ARF. Nonetheless, THE DEGREE TO WHICH SERUM CREATININE CHANGES FROM BASELINE WILL REFLECT THE CHANGE IN GFR.` The absolute value is unreliable and the definition is built on the CHANGE instead
span.quote: Like creatinine clearance, the serum creatinine will not be an accurate reflection of GFR in the non-steady-state condition of ARF. Nonetheless, the degree to which serum creatinine changes from baseline will reflect the change in GFR.

span.label: AND TREATMENT CAN MOVE A PATIENT OUT OF THE DIAGNOSTIC CLASS: `THERAPY CAN INFLUENCE THE PRIMARY CRITERIA FOR THE DIAGNOSIS OF ARF ... LARGE DOSE DIURETICS MAY BE USED TO FORCE A URINE OUTPUT WHEN IT WOULD OTHERWISE FALL INTO A CATEGORY CONSISTENT WITH A DIAGNOSIS OF ARF. Such influences are UNAVOIDABLE and ANALOGOUS TO THOSE IN OTHER DISEASE PROCESSES, which require clinical classification`
span.quote: In addition, we recognize that some of our recommendations may seem arbitrary or attempt to balance utility and precision in a way that may limit both. For example, therapy can influence the primary criteria for the diagnosis of ARF. Hydration status will influence urine output and, to some degree, may even alter the volume of distribution for creatinine. Large dose diuretics may be used to force a urine output when it would otherwise fall into a category consistent with a diagnosis of ARF. Such influences are unavoidable and analogous to those in other disease processes, which require clinical classification.

span.label: AND THE DEFINITION IS ADOPTED SO THAT ITS OWN INADEQUACY BECOMES TESTABLE: `one might hypothesize that the UNDERLYING DISEASE PROCESS that results in ARF (e.g. radiocontrast versus sepsis) WILL ALTER THE `CLINICAL MEANING` OF EACH DEGREE of renal dysfunction. However, BY APPLYING THE PRESENT CRITERIA ACROSS THESE VARIOUS AETIOLOGIES, IT WILL BE POSSIBLE TO TEST THIS HYPOTHESIS DIRECTLY.` A committee adopting a criterion it suspects is wrong, in order to find out
span.quote: Similarly, one might hypothesize that the underlying disease process that results in ARF (e.g. radiocontrast versus sepsis) will alter the 'clinical meaning' of each degree of renal dysfunction. However, by applying the present criteria across these various aetiologies, it will be possible to test this hypothesis directly.

span.label: THE DEFINITION IS PUBLISHED AS A HYPOTHESIS, WITH THE TEST NAMED: `THE ULTIMATE VALUE OF A DEFINITION FOR ARF WILL BE DETERMINED BY ITS UTILITY. A classification scheme for ARF should be SENSITIVE AND SPECIFIC, AND PREDICTIVE OF RELEVANT CLINICAL OUTCOMES such as mortality and length of hospital stay. THESE TOO ARE TESTABLE HYPOTHESES.` hoste2006 is that test, and it is in this corpus
span.quote: The ultimate value of a definition for ARF will be determined by its utility. A classification scheme for ARF should be sensitive and specific, and predictive of relevant clinical outcomes such as mortality and length of hospital stay. These too are testable hypotheses.

span.label: and the committee says where it may be arbitrary before anyone else can: `our findings should be considered a `FIRST STEP` ... the RIFLE criteria WILL NEED TO BE VALIDATED IN LARGE PATIENT SERIES - efforts that are CURRENTLY UNDERWAY`
span.quote: Indeed, it must be understood that although our recommendations are based, to the best extent possible, on data, there are insufficient data to guide many important decisions. As a result, our findings should be considered a 'first step' in the process of standardization. For example, the RIFLE criteria for diagnosis of ARF will need to be validated in large patient series – efforts that are currently underway.

span.label: THE BASELINE THE DEFINITION REQUIRES IS OFTEN ABSENT, AND THE REMEDY IS BOUNDED HERE IN A WAY THE VALIDATION LATER STRETCHED: `Note that THE MDRD FORMULA IS USED ONLY TO ESTIMATE THE BASELINE WHEN IT IS NOT KNOWN.` hoste2006 reports `APPROXIMATELY ONE-HALF OF PATIENTS WERE CLASSIFIED USING THE Cr MDRD AS A BASELINE`
span.quote: Of course, many patients may present with acute renal dysfunction without any baseline measure of renal function. This presents a problem for a system that considers the change from baseline. One option is to calculate a theoretical baseline serum creatinine value for a given patient assuming a given normal GFR. By normalizing the GFR to the body surface area, a GFR of approximately 75–100 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 can be assumed [ 15 ], and thus a change from baseline can be estimated for a given patient. The simplified 'modification of diet in renal disease' (MDRD) formula provides a robust estimate of GFR relative to serum creatinine based on age, race and sex [ 15 ]. Thus, given a patient without known renal disease but in whom a baseline creatinine is unknown, one can estimate the baseline creatinine. Table 1 solves the MDRD equation for the lower end of the normal range (i.e. 75 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 ). Note that the MDRD formula is used only to estimate the baseline when it is not known.

span.label: AND RECOVERY CANNOT BE DEFINED WITHOUT THE DEFINITION: `Recovery from ARF CAN ONLY BE EVALUATED IN THE CONTEXT OF A SPECIFIC DEFINITION OF ARF. We propose that recovery may be partial or complete` - the outcome measure inherits the classification's boundaries
span.quote: Recovery from ARF can only be evaluated in the context of a specific definition of ARF. We propose that recovery may be partial or complete. Complete renal recovery exists if the patient returns to their baseline classification within the RIFLE criteria, whereas partial renal recovery exists if there is a persistent change in RIFLE classification (R, I or F) but not persistent need for RRT.

span.label: and there is no instrument to compare against: `NO INTERNATIONALLY VALIDATED ARF-SPECIFIC SCORING SYSTEMS EXIST`, while `NO MODEL currently available PROVIDES A REPRODUCIBLE MODEL OF CLINICAL ARF as seen in the critically ill`
span.quote: Several scoring systems for assessment of organ dysfunction and morbidity have been validated in the general ICU population [ 22 - 25 ] and have also been used on ARF patients, although validation studies in the ARF setting are rare. No internationally validated ARF-specific scoring systems exist.

span.label: AND THE CLASSIFICATION EXCLUDES A POPULATION BY FIAT: `these criteria were developed to describe ARF occurring in the critically ill. PRIMARY RENAL DISEASES SUCH AS GLOMERULONEPHRITIS SHOULD BE EXCLUDED FROM THIS CLASSIFICATION SYSTEM`
span.quote: It should also be noted that these criteria were developed to describe ARF occurring in the critically ill. Primary renal diseases such as glomerulonephritis should be excluded from this classification system.

span.label: and the vote that settled disputes had a bar of its own: `When voting was required to settle an issue, A TWO-THIRDS MAJORITY was required to approve a proposal` - a third consensus threshold in this corpus, after CONSORT-AI's 80% and SITC's 75%

span.term: THE MDRD BASELINE RULE AT ITS ORIGIN IS NARROWER THAN ITS USE: `THE MDRD FORMULA IS USED ONLY TO ESTIMATE THE BASELINE WHEN IT IS NOT KNOWN`, and hoste2006 used it for about half its cohort
span.quote: Of course, many patients may present with acute renal dysfunction without any baseline measure of renal function. This presents a problem for a system that considers the change from baseline. One option is to calculate a theoretical baseline serum creatinine value for a given patient assuming a given normal GFR. By normalizing the GFR to the body surface area, a GFR of approximately 75–100 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 can be assumed [ 15 ], and thus a change from baseline can be estimated for a given patient. The simplified 'modification of diet in renal disease' (MDRD) formula provides a robust estimate of GFR relative to serum creatinine based on age, race and sex [ 15 ]. Thus, given a patient without known renal disease but in whom a baseline creatinine is unknown, one can estimate the baseline creatinine. Table 1 solves the MDRD equation for the lower end of the normal range (i.e. 75 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 ). Note that the MDRD formula is used only to estimate the baseline when it is not known.

span.term: AND RECOVERY CANNOT BE DEFINED WITHOUT THE DEFINITION: `Recovery from ARF CAN ONLY BE EVALUATED IN THE CONTEXT OF A SPECIFIC DEFINITION OF ARF`
span.quote: Recovery from ARF can only be evaluated in the context of a specific definition of ARF. We propose that recovery may be partial or complete. Complete renal recovery exists if the patient returns to their baseline classification within the RIFLE criteria, whereas partial renal recovery exists if there is a persistent change in RIFLE classification (R, I or F) but not persistent need for RRT.

span.quote: In addition to the three levels of renal dysfunction, the RIFLE (acronym indicating Risk of renal dysfunction; Injury to the kidney; Failure of kidney function, Loss of kidney function and End-stage kidney disease) criteria also include two clinical outcomes: 'loss' and 'end-stage renal disease' (ESRD). These are separated to acknowledge the important adaptations that occur in ESRD that are not seen in persistent ARF. Persistent ARF (loss) is defined as need for renal replacement therapy (RRT) for more than 4 weeks, whereas ESRD is defined by need for dialysis for longer than 3 months.

span.label: 30 — the number of competing definitions of acute renal failure this conference was convened to replace
span.quote: There is no consensus definition of acute renal failure (ARF) in critically ill patients. More than 30 different definitions have been used in the literature, creating much confusion and making comparisons difficult.

Furthermore, mortality in these populations ranges from 28% to 90% [ 10 , 11 ]. Clearly, trials of prevention and therapy are not comparable because widely disparate definitions have been used.

span.quote: However, most definitions of ARF have common elements, including the use of serum creatinine and, often, urine output. Although the kidney has numerous functions, these are the only functions that are routinely and easily measured and that are unique to the kidney.
